abstract.p: Coastal wetlands provide critical ecosystem services yet face increasing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination, and comparison of wetland microbiome responses to PFAS remains poorly resolved. Laboratory-enriched microbial consortia derived from freshwater marsh and salt marsh soils were exposed to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in 75-day microcosms at 0, 1, and 10 mg/L, then characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, phylogenetic null modeling, neutral community modeling, and KEGG-level functional prediction. Both enriched consortia showed a modest decrease in aqueous PFOA (~11–13%) at 1 mg/L but not at 10 mg/L, consistent with a potential contribution from biosorption-mediated immobilization. Incubation time dominated beta-diversity shifts (ANOSIM R > 0.90, p = 0.001), while PFOA produced no detectable compositional separation. Exploratory additive mixed-effects models indicated that alpha diversity varied primarily with microbial community source and sampling day, whereas PFOA concentration showed a nominal overall association only with Shannon diversity. Assembly analyses showed that PFOA was associated with stronger heterogeneous selection in the salt-marsh-derived consortium, whereas the freshwater-derived consortium remained stochastically dominated. When PFOA-exposed samples were pooled across both enriched consortia, the neutral community model fit collapsed (R2 < 0), signaling a regime shift toward deterministic, PFOA-mediated selection. Functionally, the salt-marsh-derived consortium showed predicted enrichment in taurine/hypotaurine metabolism and broad-spectrum proteolytic functions (serralysin and creatinase), whereas the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium showed predicted enrichment in glutathione metabolism, xenobiotic dioxygenase functions, and DNA repair pathways. Candidate PFOA-sensitive (Pseudohongiella, Flavobacterium, Parvibaculum) and PFOA-tolerant (Sericytochromatia, Legionella) taxa were identified as source-associated candidate biomarkers. Under the tested culture conditions, PFOA responses differed between the laboratory-enriched freshwater-marsh- and salt-marsh-derived bacterial consortia. These results describe source-associated responses of the enriched consortia but may need further validation with native wetland communities.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Coastal estuarine wetlands occupy the interface between marine and terrestrial environments, including mangroves, seagrass beds, and marshes [1]. Among them, freshwater and salt marshes are particularly important ecosystems because of high productivity and fast sediment deposition, and are valued for storm buffering, nutrient cycling, carbon storage, flood attenuation, water purification, and shoreline stabilization [2]. Together, these ecosystem functions support diverse plants, animals, and microbial communities and contribute to wetland biodiversity [3]. Hydrological and geological processes are among the main drivers shaping subsurface salinity, plant productivity, and the consequent ecological functions of coastal wetlands [4,5]. Under climate change, marshes with accretion rates slower than the rate of sea level rise are susceptible to inundation and submergence [6,7]. Freshwater marshes may migrate landward and be replaced by salt marshes as saltwater intrusion progresses [8]. On the other hand, terrestrially derived freshwater inputs are increasingly recognized as important sources of water and solutes to intertidal wetlands and salt marshes [9].

One of the main functions of coastal wetlands is to regulate the essential biogeochemical cycles, including organic matter decomposition, nutrient cycling, and gaseous exchanges. The soil microbiomes that inhabit these transitional terrestrial–aquatic zones experience regular or irregular inundation and pronounced gradients in structural heterogeneity, water content, pH, salinity, and organic matter [10], which affect the composition and function of microbial communities [11]. Extended flooding drives the sediments anoxic and slows organic matter decomposition [12]. In response, microbial communities accumulate biomass and accelerate the biogeochemical processes they control. The soil microbiomes have the capacity to decompose soil organic matter, facilitate sulfate reduction, oxidize sulfide/sulfur, reduce iron, perform nitrification, degrade contaminants, and contribute to the improvement of soil structure and ecosystem stability [13]. Metabolic allocations towards traits that enhance stress tolerance, such as the production of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), may inadvertently bolster carbon sequestration [14]. Additionally, microbial biochemical pathways are acutely responsive to environmental stresses, with microbial communities exhibiting reduced uptake of plant-derived carbon under conditions of heat and drought [15]. Nutrients are one of the main factors determining the activity of microbial communities and processes that regulate decomposition and nutrient cycling rates in the oligotrophic zones of coastal wetlands [16]. However, freshwater waterways can be a major source delivering nutrients from upstream, and it has been found that some archaeal groups are organo-heterotrophic for particular carbohydrates and dissolved carbon in coastal wetlands [17]. Thus, the material exchange between freshwater and salt marshes creates a dynamic ecosystem with a variety of resources (nutrients, substrates, and electron acceptors) and surroundings (such as oxygen levels and pH). Heterogeneity in resources and surroundings has a significant impact on competition between species, and diversity varies from that observed under homogeneous conditions. These changes in community richness and diversity ultimately impact ecosystem functions at the regional or global level [18].

Beyond these natural drivers, coastal ecosystems are also highly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbance [19]. For centuries, coastal wetlands and human populations have been closely intertwined, and many of these ecosystems have been progressively replaced or fragmented by agriculture, aquaculture, industry, and tourism [6]. A critical knowledge gap remains regarding the accumulation dynamics of anthropogenic compounds, such as organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), microplastics (MPs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). These contaminants are recognized as emerging but persistent pollutants in coastal marshes and their resident microflora [1]. Among pollutants, PFASs have become ubiquitous contaminants detected globally in soil, groundwater, surface water, sediments, and biota [20,21]. They have drawn attention because of their ecological, animal, and human toxicity [22,23,24,25], as well as enhanced mobility, resistance to degradation [26], bioaccumulation [27], environmental persistence [28], and long-range transport potential [29]. In coastal areas, the impacts of these contaminants on microbial communities and the subsequent ecological reverberations remain less understood than in other ecosystem types. This gap represents a critical frontier for environmental sustainability and management [30,31].

PFAS compounds have been reported to alter microbial composition, diversity, and function across diverse environments [32], whereas their biotransformation remains poorly understood owing to the difficulty of cleaving the C–F bond. Long-term PFAS exposure has been shown to significantly decrease the biodiversity of soil microbial communities and to enrich PFAS-tolerant lineages, such as Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota, and Bacteroidota [33,34]. Carbohydrate metabolism, global/overview maps, and membrane transport pathways in soil microbes are also affected by PFAS stress. Glycosyltransferases in PFAS-polluted soils were upregulated, whereas glycoside hydrolases were severely inhibited [32]. PFAS-induced perturbations to microbial community structure or function therefore carry the risk of unstable ecosystem services [33,35,36,37,38]. Field and microcosm studies have demonstrated that PFAS stress can disrupt nitrogen cycling by inhibiting genes involved in nitrification and denitrification [39,40]. Carbon cycling is similarly perturbed: PFAS exposure has been reported to transiently stimulate litter decomposition and β-glucosidase activity while inhibiting soil respiration and carbohydrate-related metabolism [37,41]. Among thousands of PFAS compounds, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is one of the most detected long-chain PFAS [42]. Owing to its extreme chemical stability, PFOA resists biotic and abiotic degradation and persists in aquatic and terrestrial environments, posing a non-negligible threat to organisms. Because coastal wetlands are heterogeneous environments increasingly affected by human activity and climate change, their indigenous microbial communities can develop high diversity and functional stability [43]. Together, these properties regulate ecosystem services and sustain water purification functions [13,44]. However, whether distinct microbial community structures emerge in coastal wetlands under PFAS stress, and what mechanisms underpin microbial resilience or adaptation, remain understudied.

To address these knowledge gaps, the present study compared the bacterial community composition, assembly patterns, and predicted functions of laboratory-enriched microbial consortia derived from freshwater marsh and salt marsh soils under PFOA exposure. The hypothesis was that the responses of these two enriched, soil-derived consortia to PFOA would depend on their inoculum source and corresponding culture conditions. To test this hypothesis, microcosms inoculated with laboratory-enriched microbial consortia derived from freshwater marsh and salt marsh soils were incubated under three PFOA concentrations (0, 1, and 10 mg/L) for 75 days, with periodic sampling for 16S rRNA gene sequencing and PFOA quantification. The study was not designed to reproduce or predict the responses of intact wetland communities under field conditions, but instead described the compositional trajectories of the enriched consortia under PFOA exposure.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Site
sec.p: The soil samples were collected along the Neponset River in the Boston area, Massachusetts, USA. The Neponset River Estuary is the section of the river where freshwater and saltwater mix, hosting 600 acres of salt marshes, managed as the Neponset River Reservation. The landward extent of the estuarine portion of the Neponset River is defined by a dam [45], and the flow is gauged by the US Geological Survey at a location just downstream from the dam to indicate the freshwater flow [46]. To capture the freshwater marsh-versus-salt marsh contrast, soil samples were collected from the freshwater marsh immediately downstream of the Baker Dam and from the salt marsh near the river mouth at Dorchester Bay, Boston Harbor (Figure S1). At both the freshwater marsh and salt marsh sites, sampling was performed at low tide within the low-marsh landscape. Soil from the 0–30 cm layer was collected at three spatially separated locations within each sampling area. The soil collected from the three locations at each site was combined and homogenized to form one composite soil sample representing that site. Background PFOA concentrations and site-specific salinity, pH, electrical conductivity, redox potential, organic carbon, and nutrient concentrations were not measured. The elevation difference between the freshwater marsh and the salt marsh is 12.71 m, and the straight-line distance between the sites is 3019 m.

sec.title: 2.2. Soil-Derived Microbial Inoculum Preparation
sec.p: The microbial inoculum was prepared from the homogenized composite soil. The surface runoff collected from the same site was filtered before use to remove microorganisms and was included to provide site-derived dissolved environmental constituents during microbial extraction. Therefore, the microbial component of the resulting inoculum was derived from the composite soil. A 10 g subsample of the homogenized composite soil and 15 mL of filtered surface runoff from each site were added to 50 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing 0.25% (w/v) sodium pyrophosphate, then vortexed to release bacterial cells from soil particles under neutral-pH buffering. Low-speed centrifugation at 500× g was used to pellet coarse debris while retaining microbial cells in the supernatant. The settled debris was washed another three times, and all supernatants were collected. The pooled supernatants were then passed through 70-μm cell strainers to remove residual particles and larger fungal hyphae and propagules. This procedure was selected to generate a particle-reduced bacterial inoculum suitable for subsequent liquid cultivation. Sodium pyrophosphate was used as a chemical dispersant to promote the release of cells from soil aggregates, while vortex mixing and low-speed centrifugation were used to separate suspended cells from coarse soil particles [47,48,49]. These procedures preferentially recovered free and loosely particle-associated bacteria but provided incomplete recovery of tightly particle-associated microorganisms [48,49]. Because the study focused on bacterial community responses using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, the preparation and subsequent analyses were designed to characterize the bacterial component of the enriched consortia rather than the complete soil microbiome. Fungi, archaea, protozoa, and other eukaryotic microorganisms were not characterized, and their presence or responses could not be evaluated.

sec.title: 2.3. Microcosms Setup
sec.p: The microcosms were established in 250-mL serum bottles containing 100 mL of culture and approximately 150 mL of ambient-air headspace. The bottles were opened in a biosafety cabinet during each sampling event and were therefore periodically re-aerated. Dissolved oxygen was not monitored during the 75-day incubation; consequently, oxygen availability between sampling events could not be reconstructed. Standard ammonium mineral salts (AMS) medium was prepared based on the formulation reported by Omer et al. (2004) [50]. The basal medium contained, per liter, 0.70 g K2HPO4, 0.54 g KH2PO4, 1.00 g MgSO4·7H2O, 0.20 g CaCl2·2H2O, 4.0 mg FeSO4·7H2O, 0.50 g NH4Cl, 100 µg ZnSO4·7H2O, 30 µg MnCl2·4H2O, 300 µg H3BO3, 200 µg CoCl2·6H2O, 10 µg CuCl2·2H2O, 20 µg NiCl2·6H2O, and 60 µg Na2MoO4·2H2O, with thiamine supplied as a vitamin supplement [50], and the pH was adjusted to 6.8. A carbon mixture was supplied to both media and contained 2 mM sodium acetate, 1.33 mM sodium propionate, 0.67 mM each of sodium benzoate, p-hydroxybenzoate, glucose, and cellobiose, and 0.167 g/L each of yeast extract and tryptone. The mixture provided organic acids, aromatic compounds, carbohydrates, and complex organic nutrients and was used to represent the organic carbon supply associated with soil total organic carbon (TOC) and to maintain microbial growth after the cells were separated from the soil matrix. Carbon availability can limit soil bacterial growth, while substrate composition and concentration can affect the recovery of heterotrophic soil microorganisms in culture. Providing this carbon mixture was therefore intended to limit community changes caused by carbon deprivation during enrichment. Defined AMS media were selected instead of filtered estuarine water to maintain known and reproducible concentrations of mineral nutrients, vitamins, and mixed carbon substrates across the PFOA treatments. Natural seawater varies spatially and temporally in its inorganic nutrients and dissolved organic matter, whereas defined artificial seawater media reduce batch-to-batch variation and improve the reproducibility of marine microbial cultivation [51,52]. Marine AMS medium is an established defined medium for cultivating microorganisms from marine sources and is commonly supplemented with 20–30 g/L NaCl [51,53], and a formulation containing 20 g/L NaCl has also been used to cultivate the model marine bacterium Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3 [53]. Accordingly, standard AMS without added NaCl was used for the freshwater-marsh-derived cultures, whereas marine AMS containing 20 g/L NaCl was used for the salt-marsh-derived cultures. The purpose was to provide standardized nutrient conditions within each source-derived culture series and a reproducible salinity contrast across the PFOA treatments rather than to recreate the complete site-specific chemistry of estuarine water. Soil-derived microbial inocula (5 mL) were diluted into the appropriate AMS medium (95 mL) at a 1:20 dilution, and biomass was monitored by optical density at 600 nm (OD600) to follow growth. When the cultures reached stationary phase (5–7 days), the suspensions were transferred into fresh medium and cultivated again. This passaging was repeated three times as a pre-exposure enrichment step to select microorganisms capable of sustained growth in standard AMS for the freshwater-derived inoculum and marine AMS supplemented with 20 g/L NaCl for the salt-marsh-derived inoculum, thereby generating controlled starting consortia for the subsequent PFOA exposure experiment. Serial enrichment and transfer in defined media are established approaches for producing simplified and comparatively stable microbial consortia suitable for controlled experiments [54,55,56]. At the same time, this selection process progressively diluted and removed some low-abundance taxa that could not maintain growth under the supplied culture conditions [55,56,57,58,59]. The enriched microbial suspension (100 mL) was then transferred into 250-mL serum bottles sealed with butyl rubber stoppers for microcosm setup. This enrichment-based design provided controlled starting communities for comparison across PFOA treatments, while direct exposure of intact field communities in their native matrices was beyond the scope of the experiment. The resulting cultures are hereafter referred to as laboratory-enriched microbial consortia derived from freshwater marsh and salt marsh soils. These consortia originated from natural soil inocula but were subsequently shaped by microbial cell extraction, cultivation in defined media, and three serial transfers. They therefore represent cultivation-selected subsets of the source communities rather than intact wetland microbiomes. The original freshwater and salt marsh soils may have differed in microbial biomass and soil characteristics. Because this was a microbe-driven study, microbial cells were extracted from the soils and cultivated in defined media to minimize the influence of these differences on the subsequent PFOA comparison. PFOA was obtained as a certified perfluoro-n-octanoic acid reference solution (CAS No. 335-67-1; molecular weight, 414.07 g/mol; Wellington Laboratories Inc., Guelph, ON, Canada; lot PFOA0824). The chemical purity was >98%, and the supplied solution had a certified concentration of 50.0 ± 2.5 µg/mL in methanol containing <1% water. According to the certificate of analysis, the reference solution also contained four molar equivalents of NaOH. The supplied 50 mg/L solution was used as the primary stock and was sequentially diluted to 5 mg/L and 100 µg/L with sterile ultrapure water. Appropriate volumes of the stock and working solutions were added to obtain nominal PFOA concentrations of 0, 1, and 10 mg/L. The 1 and 10 mg/L treatments were selected as elevated experimental exposures, and the two levels provide a 10-fold concentration contrast. They also span the range of concentrations used in previous freshwater microbial community experiments [60,61]. These concentrations were not intended to reproduce background PFOA concentrations at the sampling sites. Without the carbon mixture, carbon limitation could have caused greater changes in community composition during enrichment [62,63]. Abiotic controls were prepared identically and then autoclaved to eliminate microbial activity while preserving the same chemical matrix. Each PFOA treatment condition was established in three biological replicate microcosms. Samples from all three biological replicates were used for aqueous PFOA quantification, whereas one sequencing profile was generated for each microbial community source–PFOA concentration–sampling day condition. All bottles were incubated in the dark on an orbital shaker at 25 °C and 100 rpm for a total of 75 days. Liquid samples were collected on Days 0, 25, 50, and 75, and aliquots were stored at −20 °C until DNA extraction and PFOA quantification. Day 0 represented the enriched cultures after the three successive transfers and microcosm setup, while the original field communities were not sequenced before enrichment. During the 75-day incubation, dissolved oxygen, pH, residual carbon substrates, nutrient concentrations, microbial biomass, and extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) were not monitored.

sec.title: 2.4. PFOA Analysis
sec.p: Microbial solutions spiked with PFOA at two levels, along with abiotic controls, were centrifuged at 20,000× g for 20 min. The resulting supernatants were collected, diluted with deionized water, and spiked with 13C-PFOA as a non-extracted internal standard to a final concentration of 10 µg/L. PFOA was then quantified on an Agilent 6470 Triple Quadrupole LC–MS/MS system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) in negative electrospray multiple-reaction monitoring (MRM) mode. Aqueous PFOA was quantified in three biological replicate microcosms per treatment condition, and each biological replicate was measured in analytical triplicate by LC–MS/MS. Aqueous PFOA concentrations were calculated relative to the 13C-PFOA internal standard response [64].

sec.title: 2.5. DNA Extraction and 16S rRNA Gene Sequencing and Analysis
sec.p: A 10-mL aliquot of each culture was centrifuged at 10,000× g for 10 min, and the supernatant was discarded to concentrate the biomass into a cell pellet. DNA concentrations in the discarded supernatants were not measured. The sequencing workflow therefore targeted biomass-associated DNA recovered from the pellet, whereas extracellular DNA remaining in the discarded liquid phase was not included. Genomic DNA was extracted from the biomass pellet using the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Environmental DNA comprises both intracellular and extracellular fractions, and the relative contribution of extracellular DNA varies among microbial systems [65,66]. Because DNA in the discarded supernatant was not measured, the sequencing profiles represent pellet-associated bacterial DNA rather than the complete intracellular-plus-extracellular DNA pool. DNA concentrations were quantified on a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) prior to library preparation. The sequencing libraries were prepared using the 2 × 250 bp kit. The targeted V3–V4 regions of 16S rRNA genes were amplified using the following primers: 16S 341F (5′-CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3′) and 16S 785R (5′-GACTACHVGGGTATCTAATCC-3′). After barcoding and indexing, the library was circularized and sequenced on the Illumina platform. The Bases2Fastq software (v1.4.0; Element Biosciences, San Diego, CA, USA) was used to convert the bases files into FASTQ files and de-multiplex the pooled library based on index sequences. Data processing was performed following the established Mothur protocol (software version 1.48.2) [67,68]. After removal of barcodes, primer sequences, low-quality reads, and chimeras, the remaining amplicon reads were rarefied to the minimum sequencing depth across samples to minimize biases associated with uneven coverage [69]. Operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were generated at a 97% sequence identity threshold and taxonomically classified against the SILVA reference database (Release 138.2), and the same rarefied OTU table was used as input for both the diversity and Tax4Fun2 functional prediction analyses to ensure internal consistency.

sec.title: 2.6. Microbial Function Prediction
sec.p: Putative functional traits of each sample were predicted using the Tax4Fun2 R package [70] by analyzing enzyme genes and metabolic pathways based on microbial profiles with taxonomic information. Briefly, the representative sequence of each OTU was queried against the KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) database, in which functional profiles are linked to genome-level taxonomic keys, using a uclust identity threshold of 100% (“Ref100NR” mode). The OTU abundance table from the final step of the Mothur pipeline (97% identity threshold, species level) was then used to map functional profiles to each OTU [71]. Tax4Fun2 outputs comprised relative abundance tables of KEGG level 3 pathways and individual enzymes (EC numbers), which were used for the downstream functional analyses.

sec.title: 2.7. Bacterial Community Assembly Mechanism
sec.p: Community assembly mechanisms were further evaluated using the beta-nearest taxon index (βNTI), which partitions the relative contributions of stochastic and deterministic processes in community turnover. These processes are partitioned into five categories: heterogeneous selection, homogeneous selection, homogenizing dispersal, dispersal limitation, and drift (including other undetermined processes) [72]. Within this framework, a value of |βNTI| > 2 indicates that deterministic processes dominate community turnover, with βNTI > +2 reflecting heterogeneous selection (different environmental filters selecting for different phylogenetic clades) and βNTI < −2 reflecting homogeneous selection (similar filters selecting for similar clades). Moreover, |βNTI| ≤ 2 reveals the dominance of stochastic processes, indicating that the turnover of the bacterial community is governed by dispersal limitation, homogenizing dispersal, or other undetermined processes. To further evaluate the importance of stochastic processes, a neutral community model (NCM) was fitted to relate the detection frequency of each OTU to its mean relative abundance across the broader metacommunity [73]. In general, the model predicts that taxa that are abundant in the metacommunity will be widespread, since they are more likely to disperse by chance among different sampling sites. In contrast, rare taxa are more likely to be lost in different sites due to ecological drift (i.e., the stochastic loss and replacement of individuals) [74]. Hmisc (version 5.0.1), minpack.lm (version 1.2.3), and getopt (version 1.20.3) packages in R were used for the NCM.

sec.title: 2.8. Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Temporal compositional stability was quantified using the average variation degree (AVD) following Xun et al. (2021) [59]. For genus i in sample j, the standardized variation degree was calculated as:aij=|xij−x¯i|δi where xij is the relative abundance of genus i in sample j, x¯i is its mean relative abundance across the samples included in the same microbiome–PFOA treatment group, and δi is the corresponding standard deviation. The community-level AVD was then calculated as:AVD=1kn∑j=1k∑i=1naij where k is the number of samples in the treatment group, and n is the number of genera. AVD therefore represents the mean standardized deviation of genus-level relative abundances from their group means. Lower AVD values indicate smaller community-wide compositional fluctuations and greater temporal compositional stability, whereas higher values indicate greater temporal turnover. In this study, stability refers specifically to compositional constancy during the post-enrichment incubation period and excludes functional stability, resistance, or recovery following disturbance.

Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was performed to compare community similarity based on weighted UniFrac distances computed from the rarefied OTU table [75], using the phyloseq R package [76]. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) was used to identify taxa most likely to explain differences among groups (PFOA concentrations or sampling days), based on the non-parametric factorial Kruskal–Wallis sum-rank test followed by the (unpaired) Wilcoxon rank-sum test [77]. The determining taxon was defined as the representative biomarker of the specific group [78]. For each sequencing-derived alpha diversity metric (Sobs, Shannon, Simpson, ACE, Chao1, and Good’s coverage), an exploratory additive linear mixed-effects model was fitted to observations from Days 25, 50, and 75. Microbial community source, PFOA concentration, and sampling day were included as fixed effects. A random intercept was included for each of the six source–concentration series to account for repeated observations over time. Day 0 was excluded because it represented a source-specific background measured before assignment to the PFOA treatments. Given the limited number of sequencing profiles and the absence of within-condition sequencing replication, the models were restricted to additive main effects and excluded interaction terms. Overall fixed effects were evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests. Fixed-effect estimates were standardized by the observed standard deviation of each diversity metric to permit comparison among metrics. Because the estimated random intercept variance approached zero, the model estimates and nominal p-values were interpreted as exploratory. One-way ANOVA followed by the Tukey–Kramer post-hoc test was applied across comparable samples to evaluate the statistical significance of differences in taxon abundances and predicted functional pathways. The p-values from the multiple ANOSIM and Kruskal–Wallis comparisons were adjusted for the false discovery rate (Benjamini–Hochberg). All statistical analyses were performed in R with significance reported at α = 0.05 unless otherwise stated.

sec.title: 3.1. Decrease in Aqueous PFOA
sec.p: Aqueous PFOA concentrations were monitored under the two spiking levels (1 and 10 mg/L) over the 75-day incubation in both enriched consortia and in autoclaved abiotic controls (Figure 1). A modest decrease in aqueous PFOA concentration was observed only at the 1 mg/L exposure level, whereas no clear decreasing trend relative to Day 0 was observed at 10 mg/L in either microbial treatment. At Day 75 under the 1 mg/L treatment, freshwater-derived consortia achieved a marginally higher reduction in aqueous PFOA (≈13%) than salt-marsh-derived consortia (≈11%) relative to their respective Day 0 values, while abiotic controls showed no comparable decrease. Because transformation products and fluoride release were not measured, this decrease should not be interpreted as evidence of PFOA biodegradation. In contrast, abiotic controls retained 95–100% of their initial aqueous PFOA across the 75-day incubation at both concentrations, indicating that biomass-associated processes may have contributed to the modest aqueous PFOA decrease observed in biotic treatments. At Day 25, the mean aqueous PFOA concentration in some biotic treatments was slightly higher than the corresponding Day 0 value. No statistical comparison was performed specifically between Day 0 and Day 25, and therefore, this apparent increase should not be interpreted as statistically significant. The available measurements were unable to distinguish technical variation arising from sample preparation and LC–MS/MS analysis from redistribution of PFOA between the aqueous and biomass-associated phases.

sec.title: 3.2.1. Microbial Diversity
sec.p: At Day 0, the freshwater-derived inoculum exhibited slightly higher richness and diversity (observed species, Sobs = 348; Shannon H’ = 3.34) than the salt-marsh-derived inoculum (Sobs = 307; Shannon H’ = 3.05) (Table S1). In the absence of PFOA (0 mg/L controls), both enriched consortia underwent substantial temporal restructuring. Diversity in both the salt marsh and freshwater marsh controls increased from Day 0 to Day 50, peaking with Shannon indices of 4.42 and 4.55, respectively. By Day 75, however, diversity in both control groups declined, with Shannon indices falling to ~3.2 in both enriched consortia. This suggests that the microcosm incubation conditions themselves induced major structural shifts in both enriched consortia, especially between Day 50 and Day 75. Across the post-enrichment observations from Days 25 to 75, the exploratory additive mixed-effects models indicated nominal overall effects of microbial community source on Sobs (p < 0.001), Shannon diversity (p < 0.001), Simpson diversity (p < 0.001), ACE richness (p = 0.012), and Chao richness (p = 0.009). In contrast, no nominal overall effect of source was detected on Good’s coverage (p = 0.257). Sampling day was also associated with Sobs (p = 0.008), Shannon diversity (p < 0.001), Simpson diversity (p < 0.001), ACE richness (p = 0.006), and Chao richness (p = 0.003), but not with Good’s coverage (p = 0.153). PFOA concentration showed a nominal overall association only with Shannon diversity (p = 0.027), while no nominal overall concentration association was detected for the other alpha diversity metrics (p ≥ 0.104) (Figure S2A).

For Shannon diversity, the model-estimated marginal means were 4.46 for the freshwater-derived consortium and 3.97 for the salt-marsh-derived consortium. The corresponding marginal means were 4.10, 4.32, and 4.24 at 0, 1, and 10 mg/L PFOA, respectively, and 4.33, 4.51, and 3.81 on Days 25, 50, and 75, respectively (Figure S2B–D). Because the estimated random intercept variance approached zero, these estimates were treated as exploratory and are unable to provide confirmatory evidence of source-dependent PFOA responses.

sec.title: 3.2.2. Microbial Community Stability
sec.p: The average variation degree (AVD) was used to summarize community-wide temporal fluctuation across all measured time points, as described in Section 2.8. Lower AVD values indicate greater temporal compositional stability, whereas higher values indicate greater temporal turnover. In this analysis, “stability” refers only to temporal variation across the post-enrichment sampling period, while compositional similarity between the enriched cultures and the original field communities was not assessed. Since the measure of stability is over an entire time course, the most direct and standard interpretation comes from the data grouped by PFOA concentration (Figure S3). After the initial adaptation period, the presence of PFOA at either 1 mg/L or 10 mg/L had no significant impact on the overall temporal stability of the salt-marsh-derived consortium compared to the control. All experimental groups displayed similarly elevated AVD values, indicating comparably high temporal turnover. Similarly, PFOA exposure had no effect on the temporal stability of the freshwater-derived consortium, with AVD values comparable across all treatment groups. Therefore, the inherent turnover associated with microcosm incubation dominated the temporal dynamics, but PFOA produced no detectable increase in this turnover. The AVD results suggest that the inherent instability of the laboratory setup was a more powerful influence on community dynamics than the chemical stress from PFOA. Neither community’s temporal stability was measurably decreased by the presence of PFOA over the experimental period.

sec.title: 3.2.3. Microbial Community Composition
sec.p: In both the freshwater- and salt-marsh-derived consortia, incubation time was the strongest factor shaping genus-level community composition (Figure 2A,B). Genus-level community dynamics across PFOA and time showed clear seed-dependent trajectories. The freshwater-derived consortium was broadly dominated by Pseudomonadota, Actinobacteriota, and Firmicutes, with persistent high-abundance taxa such as Nitrosomonas, Bradyrhizobium, Simplicispira, and Rhodanobacter. Several genera nonetheless showed time- and dose-associated shifts: Pseudomonas peaked early (Day 25) and declined by Days 50–75, whereas taxa such as Legionella increased toward later time points (Days 50–75) across treatments, indicating progressive restructuring during incubation rather than a single immediate PFOA shock response. In contrast, the salt-marsh-derived consortium was dominated by marine- and coastal-associated Pseudomonadota and Bacteroidota, with consistently high signal from Pseudomonas and Hydrogenophaga across conditions. A pronounced late-stage enrichment of initially low-abundance Alphaproteobacteria and Microbacteriaceae lineages emerged by Day 75, particularly under PFOA-spiked treatments, suggesting a delayed, dose-amplified selection process. The Circos biplots of the top 5% of genera (Figure 2C,D) confirmed that the same dominant taxa repeatedly formed the compositional backbone of each community across all PFOA conditions over time. The relative share of secondary taxa and the other bacteria fraction varied across sampling days, indicating reweighting within a stable dominant set rather than wholesale turnover. In the salt-marsh-derived consortium, the most pronounced late-stage redistribution occurred among Rhodobacteraceae-related lineages by Day 75, consistent with the dose-amplified selection process inferred from the heatmap.

sec.title: 3.2.4. Microbial Community Similarity
sec.p: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) on weighted UniFrac distances was used to visualize community-level similarity among samples (Figure 3). Group separation was tested by analysis of similarities (ANOSIM), reporting the R statistic and associated p-value. PCoA ordination revealed that incubation time was the dominant driver of beta diversity, whereas PFOA concentration (0, 1, 10 mg/L) produced no detectable compositional separation in either seed microbiome. In the freshwater-derived consortium, samples showed no separation by PFOA dose (ANOSIM R = −0.2263, p = 0.873) but strong separation by sampling day (R = 0.9753, p = 0.001). The day-grouped ordination was dominated by PC1 (71.29%) and PC2 (13.82%), consistent with a pronounced temporal trajectory across the 75-day incubation. The salt-marsh-derived consortium showed the same pattern that no separation by PFOA concentration (R = −0.2510, p = 0.855) but clear grouping by day (R = 0.9095, p = 0.001), with the ordination dominated by PC1 (77.03%) and PC2 (17.22%) in the day-grouped plot. The large fraction of variance captured along PC1 (>70%) in both enriched consortia, together with sampling order, is consistent with a directional, succession-like trajectory, motivating the null-model analyses (Section 3.3).

A supervised partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) was applied to identify genus-level features that best separated the predefined PFOA treatment groups (Figure S4). PLS-DA revealed a distinct separation between the control group (0 mg/L) and the two PFOA-treated groups (1 and 10 mg/L). This separation occurred primarily along the COMP1 axis, which explains 13.13% of the variance. All control samples had negative values on the COMP1 axis, while nearly all PFOA-exposed samples had positive values. The 1 mg/L (light blue triangles) and 10 mg/L (dark green diamonds) groups largely overlapped with each other on the right side of the plot. No clear separation was observed between the two PFOA concentrations, indicating that the genus-level signature of PFOA exposure was qualitatively similar across the two doses tested.

sec.title: 3.3.1. Community Assembly Process
sec.p: To partition the relative contributions of deterministic and stochastic processes to community assembly, a phylogenetic null-model framework based on the beta-nearest taxon index (βNTI) was applied (Figure 4). In both enriched consortia (Figure 4B,C), Day 50 and Day 75 turnover was attributed almost entirely to drift and other undetermined processes (~1.0), indicating that incubation-driven succession became overwhelmingly stochastic at the later stages of the experiment. At Day 0, both enriched consortia showed substantial heterogeneous selection (~0.45) and an additional dispersal limitation component (~0.20–0.25), with drift accounting for the remainder, indicating strong initial niche differentiation and dispersal constraint in the starting inocula. When summarized by PFOA concentration (Figure 4A), the freshwater-derived consortium remained largely drift-dominated at 0 and 1 mg/L (with smaller contributions from heterogeneous selection and dispersal limitation), whereas at 10 mg/L drift increased further, with dispersal limitation persisting as the primary non-drift component. In contrast, the salt-marsh-derived consortium exhibited a dose-amplified deterministic signature. Heterogeneous selection became the dominant process at 1 mg/L and remained substantial at 10 mg/L, indicating that PFOA imposed markedly stronger niche-based filtering on the salt-marsh-derived consortium than on the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium under the same exposure regime. Overall, incubation time drove both enriched consortia toward stochastic assembly, but PFOA imposed a comparatively stronger, seed-dependent deterministic signature on the salt-marsh-derived consortium, consistent with greater sensitivity of its phylogenetic turnover to PFAS stress. These assembly patterns differed between the two enriched consortia, however, they should not be interpreted as confirmation of source-dependent PFOA effects on alpha diversity because source × PFOA interactions could not be evaluated in the alpha diversity analysis.

sec.title: 3.3.2. Neutral Community Model
sec.p: The neutral community model (NCM) developed by Sloan et al. quantifies the fraction of community structure that can be explained by stochastic dispersal and ecological drift in microbial systems [73]. When each seed microbiome was modeled independently, the NCM explained a large fraction of the occurrence–abundance relationship (R2 = 0.87 for the freshwater-derived consortium, and R2 = 0.89 for the salt-marsh-derived consortium; Figure 5A,B). However, this neutral fit collapsed when PFOA-exposed samples (1 and 10 mg/L) were pooled across both seed microbiomes (R2 = −0.85; Figure 5C). The migration rate (m) was higher in the freshwater-derived consortium (m = 1.13) than in the salt-marsh-derived consortium (m = 0.85), indicating weaker dispersal limitation and more efficient exchange of taxa between the metacommunity and local microcosms in the freshwater system. A larger fraction of OTUs in the salt-marsh-derived consortium fell below the 95% confidence interval of the neutral prediction, indicating that more taxa are under environmental filtering or selective pressure, consistent with the lower m value. The effective dispersal parameter (Nm) quantifies the strength of dispersal from the metacommunity to the local communities. The higher Nm of the freshwater-derived consortium is consistent with a more open assemblage with greater microbial exchange, whereas the salt-marsh-derived consortium experienced stronger dispersal filtering. The lower migration rate and stronger dispersal limitation of the salt-marsh-derived community indicate a source-associated difference in community assembly. Salinity and osmotic stress can affect microbial dispersal and assembly in saline environments.

sec.title: 3.3.3. Potential Biomarker Taxa Identification
sec.p: To identify potential microbial biomarkers of PFOA exposure, the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis H test was applied across PFOA concentrations after pooling samples regardless of sampling day (Figure 6A,D). In the salt-marsh-derived consortium, OTU98 (Pseudohongiella), OTU304 (Flavobacterium), OTU439 and OTU428 (Parvibaculum), OTU66 (Edaphobaculum), and OTU65 (uncultured KD4-96) showed their highest relative abundance in the control (0 mg/L) and decreased in the presence of PFOA. These taxa are therefore candidate PFOA-sensitive lineages in this enriched consortium, whereas no genus was significantly enriched at 10 mg/L PFOA in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. In contrast, OTU627 (uncultured Sericytochromatia) in the freshwater-derived consortium showed a clear increase in relative abundance at 10 mg/L, suggesting tolerance to or even a competitive advantage under high-PFOA exposure.

To further track the temporal emergence of biomarkers, pairwise Fisher’s exact tests were used to compare OTU abundances between successive sampling days (Day 25 vs. Day 50; Day 50 vs. Day 75) under 10 mg/L PFOA (Figure 6B,C,E,F). In the salt-marsh-derived consortium, only OTU498 (uncultured Terasakiellaceae) showed a sustained significant enrichment across both intervals. In the freshwater-derived consortium, two Legionella OTUs (OTU593 and OTU426) were progressively enriched across both intervals under 10 mg/L PFOA. These progressively enriched lineages are promising candidate microbial biomarkers of sustained PFOA exposure in their respective enriched consortia.

sec.title: 3.4.1. Predicted Pathways
sec.p: Across all KEGG level 3 pathway predictions, the two seed microbiomes exhibited markedly distinct functional baselines, with smaller within-seed shifts attributable to time or PFOA dose. When comparing salt marsh vs. freshwater marsh (averaged across all timepoints and concentrations, Table S2), the salt-marsh-derived consortium showed higher predicted representation of pathways largely assigned to glycan/lipid-related metabolism and secondary metabolite modules, including fatty acid elongation (ko00062) and multiple glycan biosynthesis pathways (e.g., N-glycan biosynthesis/various N-glycan/O-glycan and glycosphingolipid biosynthesis; ko00513/ko00515/ko00604/ko00510). Predicted representation of flavone/flavonol biosynthesis (ko00944) was also higher. In contrast, the freshwater-derived consortium showed higher predicted representation of several pathways annotated under cellular processes/replication–repair and xenobiotic/secondary metabolism, including furfural degradation (ko00365) and multiple terpenoid/polyketide-related modules (e.g., monoterpenoid biosynthesis ko00902; sesquiterpenoid/triterpenoid biosynthesis ko00909), along with DNA-repair-linked functions (e.g., non-homologous end joining ko03450). Together, these predicted profiles indicate greater representation of membrane- and glycan-associated functions in the salt-marsh-derived consortium and of stress response, DNA repair, and xenobiotic transformation functions in the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium under the same incubation design.

ANOVA with Tukey–Kramer post-hoc tests showed that three focal pathways differed primarily by seed microbiome rather than by PFOA dose, with similar patterns for several glycan and secondary metabolite biosynthesis pathways (Figure 7 and Figure S5). Collectively, the predicted potentials for β-lactam-resistance and glutathione-mediated redox buffering were significantly higher in the freshwater-derived consortium, whereas sulfur- and osmolyte-associated metabolism (taurine/hypotaurine) was significantly higher in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. Seed microbiome identity was the dominant driver of the differences in all three pathways, with PFOA concentration producing only smaller, context-dependent modulation of these seed-defined baselines.

sec.title: 3.4.2. Predicted Enzymes
sec.p: Across the enzyme prediction tables, the two seed microbiomes showed clear seed-dependent functional baselines, with a subset of enzymes consistently higher in salt marsh versus freshwater marsh (and vice versa) across the full time × PFOA design (Table S3). Salt-marsh-enriched enzymes (Table S3) included redox and carbon–nitrogen-related functions such as lactaldehyde reductase (EC 1.1.1.77), isobutyryl-CoA mutase (EC 5.4.99.13), and guanidinopropionase (EC 3.5.3.17), indicating a stronger predicted capacity for specific aldehyde/CoA transformations and guanidino-compound turnover in the salt-derived community. In contrast, freshwater-derived consortia (Table S3) showed higher predicted representation of multiple oxygenase and xenobiotic-associated enzymes, including limonene 1,2-monooxygenase (EC 1.14.13.107) and phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase (EC 1.14.12.7), consistent with greater predicted potential for oxidative transformation pathways in the freshwater inoculum. Overall, these predicted enzyme-level patterns mirrored the pathway-level results: source microbiome (salt vs. freshwater) explained the dominant functional separation, while time and PFOA were associated with smaller differences in predicted enzyme proportions within that seed-defined backdrop.

Within each seed microbiome, PFOA produced only modest shifts in predicted enzyme profiles over the 75-day incubation, especially when compared with the much larger baseline differences between salt-marsh-derived and freshwater-derived consortia. When restricting to the most abundant enzymes (top quartile by mean abundance), the typical maximum change attributable to PFOA (comparing 1 vs. 0 and 10 vs. 0 mg/L across all sampling days) was small, with median max shifts of ~0.15 log2 in salt marsh and ~0.14 log2 in freshwater (≈10–11% change), and even the extreme abundant-enzyme responses remained limited (99th percentile ~0.63 log2 in salt marsh and ~0.57 log2 in freshwater marsh). The clearest within-seed responses were enzyme-specific and time-dependent: in salt marsh, the largest PFOA-associated shifts among abundant enzymes were observed for xylulokinase (EC 2.7.1.17) and quinone oxidoreductase (EC 1.8.5.4) (strongest at 10 vs. 0 mg/L on Day 25). Asparagine synthase (EC 6.3.5.4) also showed one of the largest shifts (notable at 1 vs. 0 mg/L on Day 75). In freshwater marsh, the strongest abundant-enzyme shifts were concentrated early (Day 25), including mono(ethylene terephthalate) hydrolase (EC 3.1.1.102), aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.19), and phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase (EC 1.14.12.7) (often peaking at 1 vs. 0 mg/L). A smaller late response was observed for ribosome biogenesis GTPase/thiamine phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.100) at 10 vs. 0 mg/L on Day 75. Overall, these patterns suggest that PFOA was not associated with broad changes in predicted enzyme functional potential within either seed over this timescale, and the observed differences were limited to a small subset of enzymes and varied among sampling times.

sec.title: 3.4.3. The Variation of Pathways and Enzymes
sec.p: The majority of significantly differential predicted enzymes (11 of 16) had consistently higher predicted relative abundance in the salt-marsh-derived consortium than in the freshwater-derived consortium (Figure S6). These salt-marsh-enriched predicted functions were associated with complex macromolecular substrates. In particular, serralysin (EC 3.4.24.40) and creatinase (EC 3.5.3.3) had considerably higher predicted relative abundances in the salt-marsh-derived consortium than in the freshwater-derived consortium, and their predicted proportions tended to increase under PFOA exposure in the salt-marsh-derived consortium (Figure S6). Overall, the predicted enzyme profiles of the two microbial communities were fundamentally distinct. The salt-marsh-derived consortium showed higher predicted representation of enzymes associated with the degradation of complex substrates such as proteins, and this representation tended to increase under PFOA exposure. In contrast, the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium showed higher predicted representation of a different set of redox and biosynthetic enzymes, several of which also differed across PFOA treatments, indicating contrasting predicted functional profiles between the two source communities. Consistent with the taxonomic shifts (Section 3.2.3) and assembly contrast (Section 3.3), the enzyme-level patterns showed predicted enrichment in extracellular proteolysis and osmolyte-associated functions in the salt-marsh-derived consortium and in oxidative xenobiotic transformation and redox buffering functions in the freshwater-derived consortium. Because dissolved oxygen was not monitored, the contribution of changes in oxygen availability to these predicted functional profiles could not be separated from the PFOA-associated patterns.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: This study examines how the bacterial components of laboratory-enriched microbial consortia derived from freshwater marsh and salt marsh soils responded to PFOA at the levels of taxonomy, community assembly, and predicted function. Serial cultivation can select microorganisms suited to the supplied growth conditions and alter community composition [58]. These cultures were generated through a top-down enrichment procedure using natural environmental inocula and therefore differ from synthetic communities assembled from selected isolates. Nevertheless, cultivation in defined media and serial transfer may impose strong selection. The resulting consortia should not be treated as intact representations of the source wetland microbiomes. Even so, this design followed previous enrichment-based work, where natural soil inocula were grown and serially transferred in defined media to yield tractable consortia for controlled experiments. The inoculum preparation procedure introduced an additional source of selection because pyrophosphate dispersion, low-speed centrifugation, and 70-μm straining preferentially recovered suspended and loosely particle-associated bacteria, while tightly particle-associated cells and larger fungal structures may have been depleted [48,49]. These consortia retained taxa and compositional features associated with their source soils, but cultivation and serial transfer selected a reduced subset of the original communities and progressively washed out some low-abundance taxa [55,56]. Because low-abundance taxa can make disproportionate contributions to microbial community function, the taxa lost during enrichment may contain ecologically important organisms, including potential contributors to PFOA transformation. The findings therefore describe responses of enriched cultures but not the in-situ wetland microbiomes. Supplying the carbon mixture as a proxy for the organic carbon associated with soil TOC was intended to sustain microbial growth and to avoid community changes associated with carbon deprivation [62,63]. Direct exposure experiments using unmanipulated field communities would be needed to determine whether the observed responses also occur within native wetland matrices. Because dissolved oxygen, pH, residual carbon substrates, nutrient concentrations, microbial biomass, and EPS were not monitored during incubation, their potential contributions to microbial community dynamics and PFOA adsorption could not be evaluated, and a complete PFOA mass balance could not be established. The sequencing profiles represent DNA recovered from the centrifuged biomass pellets. Because DNA in the discarded supernatants was not measured, the contribution of extracellular DNA released into the liquid phase could not be quantified. The carbon mixture was supplied as the carbon source, and carbon-mixture-free controls were not included. The independent contribution of carbon-supported growth to the observed taxonomic and diversity patterns therefore could not be separated from the effects of PFOA exposure.

Moreover, the salt-marsh-derived cultures were maintained in marine AMS containing 20 g/L NaCl, whereas the freshwater-marsh-derived cultures were maintained in AMS without added NaCl. The experimental design is therefore unable to separate the effect of microbiome source from that of culture salinity. Accordingly, the observed differences are interpreted as contrasts between the two source-derived consortia under their respective culture conditions. The contributions of prior PFOA exposure and specific site environmental factors to the community differences and PFOA responses cannot be resolved from the available data. Multicountry monitoring studies illustrate the variability of PFOA concentrations in surface waters. Baabish et al. (2021) quantified PFOA at 0.05–4.02 ng/L in 144 surface water samples from 22 countries, while Kunacheva et al. (2012) reported city-average river water concentrations of 0.2–1630.2 ng/L across 41 cities in 15 countries, with higher concentrations in industrialized areas [54,79]. For regulatory context, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established an enforceable maximum contaminant level of 4.0 ng/L for PFOA in drinking water (U.S. EPA, 2024) [80]. Although this standard applies to drinking water rather than wetland soil or surface water, it further illustrates the substantial difference between regulatory-scale concentrations and the 1–10 mg/L treatments used in this study. A point worth addressing explicitly is the gap between the PFOA concentrations used here (1 and 10 mg/L) and the ng/L–μg/L levels typical of background coastal surface waters. The deliberate use of elevated doses in microcosm experiments is, however, an approach used in PFAS microbial ecology studies [60,61] for several reasons. PFOA-induced microbial growth inhibition and cellular stress have been documented in laboratory experiments [81]. First, microbial community responses, such as taxonomic reshuffling, assembly regime shifts, and predicted functional re-allocation, can be examined under elevated PFOA exposure alongside the strong incubation-driven succession signal documented here (Section 3.2 and Section 3.3). Previous freshwater community experiments have examined responses at 5 and 10 mg/L PFOA [60,61], while the exposure duration needed to generate comparable community-level signatures at ng/L concentrations was not assessed in the present study. Second, microbial communities at the sediment-water interface and in EPS-rich biofilms may encounter PFOA associated with the biofilm matrix, as PFOA binding to sludge EPS proteins has been characterized, and PFOA has been measured in natural river biofilms at 463.73 ± 601.16 ng/g wet weight (n = 3) [82,83]. These processes provide a mechanistic context for microbial exposure, although a 1–10 mg/L aqueous treatment in the present microcosms cannot be directly equated with local microbe-scale exposure under chronic, lower aqueous contamination. Finally, the two doses (1 vs. 10 mg/L) provide a 10-fold exposure contrast. At 1 mg/L, the observed decrease in aqueous PFOA was consistent with a possible contribution from biosorption; the same pattern was not detected at 10 mg/L. This concentration-dependent difference provides a basis for comparing microbial responses between the two treatments. The magnitudes and directions of the responses observed at 1 and 10 mg/L are specific to the enriched consortia and the tested culture conditions and should not be extrapolated to chronic field exposure at ng/L–µg/L concentrations. Analytical resolution was an additional practical consideration in selecting elevated exposure concentrations. At ng/L exposure levels, small temporal changes in aqueous PFOA could be comparable to the sampling and analytical variability of the present experimental design, whereas the mg/L treatments provided a concentration contrast that could be resolved more reliably.

Both enriched consortia attenuated aqueous PFOA concentrations only modestly, with a measurable decrease restricted to the lower 1 mg/L exposure and no detectable reduction at 10 mg/L. Both the magnitude and the concentration dependence of these dynamics are consistent with potential biosorption-dominated immobilization, possibly involving association of PFOA with the extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix and adsorption to microbial cell surfaces [84]. Prior work observed increased secretion of tryptophan-like and humic-like fluorescent components in response to PFOA, consistent with the active production of EPS as a protective barrier that fortuitously immobilized the toxicant [84]. Consistent with this possible explanation, microalgal-mediated bioremediation by Scenedesmus quadricauda was shown to remove 44.8% of PFOA via bioaccumulation and 12.8% via bioabsorption, with only 0.58% biodegraded after 30 days [85]. The small magnitude of the difference in removal between the two source-derived consortia is consistent with a possible role for physicochemical partitioning in the observed aqueous PFOA attenuation. Under high-salinity conditions, divalent cations and elevated ionic strength promote partitioning of PFOA onto the solid phase. This partitioning may dampen aqueous PFOA exposure and the resulting selective pressure on microbial populations [86]. If PFOA loss were driven by passive equilibrium partitioning to biomass, removal would depend on the available sorbent surface and the partitioning behavior at each loading. The absence of a measurable decrease at 10 mg/L may reflect PFOA suppression of the active biomass and EPS production involved in immobilization, consistent with prior reports that elevated PFOA compromises membrane integrity and reduces bacterial viability [81]. The observed values describe a decrease in aqueous PFOA concentration, with biosorption and phase partitioning considered possible contributing processes. Phase-resolved PFOA measurements, transformation product analysis, and fluoride release measurements would be needed to evaluate these processes [87].

The exploratory alpha diversity analysis indicated that microbial community source and sampling day were the principal correlates of richness and diversity, whereas PFOA concentration showed a nominal overall association only with Shannon diversity. The model-estimated Shannon mean was lower for the salt-marsh-derived consortium than for the freshwater-derived consortium and varied across the post-enrichment sampling days. Because interaction terms were not included in the additive models, the apparent source-specific concentration patterns cannot establish that PFOA increased diversity in one consortium while suppressing it in the other. Salinity and tidal variability can impose osmotic stress on salt marsh microbial communities. Such background constraints may increase sensitivity to an additional stressor such as PFOA, although their contribution could not be evaluated without site-specific physicochemical measurements [88]. This is consistent with the decline of marine-associated genera such as Pseudohongiella and Flavobacterium in the salt-marsh-derived consortium under PFOA exposure, leaving a simplified community dominated by a smaller set of specialized and tolerant taxa. Within the tested enriched consortia, the contrasting diversity responses were associated with microbiome source and culture conditions. Their relevance to the stress tolerance of native wetland communities remains unresolved. In addition, carbon substrates and the different AMS formulations may also have contributed to the observed diversity patterns through cultivation-related selection. Because carbon-free controls were not included, the contributions of carbon supplementation, culture salinity, and PFOA exposure cannot be separated in the present design.

The source-specific patterns observed in the unadjusted Shannon profiles may be consistent with a competitive-release mechanism, although this interpretation remains hypothetical because source × PFOA interactions could not be tested in the present design. In the freshwater-derived consortium, the incubation-driven decline of dominant Pseudomonadota, exemplified by the time-dominant Pseudomonas lineage, may have opened niche space that was further modified under PFOA exposure. That niche space may have allowed previously rare but tolerant lineages to expand, such as the OTU627 Sericytochromatia genotype identified as a candidate PFOA-associated taxon in the freshwater-derived consortium (Figure 6). The community thus appeared more diverse under PFOA, possibly not because growth was stimulated in absolute terms, but because PFOA-tolerant rare lineages may have been able to fill the niches opened by incubation-driven succession. In the salt-marsh-derived community, the baseline composition may have been shaped by both the source environment and the saline culture medium. PFOA-associated declines in sensitive marine-associated taxa (Pseudohongiella, Flavobacterium, Parvibaculum) may have contributed to the observed decrease in Shannon diversity. This possible competitive-release interpretation is qualitatively consistent with the assembly evidence that the freshwater-derived consortium remained drift-dominated under PFOA, signaling sustained stochastic replacement of disturbed positions, whereas the salt-marsh-derived consortium shifted into heterogeneous, niche-based selection, indicating that only a subset of pre-adapted genotypes could occupy the post-disturbance space.

The intrinsic temporal trajectory of microcosm incubation, driven by nutrient drawdown and competition, can produce a strong temporal signal that overshadows more subtle contaminant-driven effects on beta diversity [89,90]. The present finding that incubation time was a far stronger driver of beta diversity than PFOA concentration aligns with these observations and reinforces the value of time-resolved sampling for distinguishing incubation-driven succession from PFOA-associated changes [91]. PFOA can inhibit microbial growth under laboratory exposure conditions [61], but the present data are insufficient to establish that biomass inhibition caused the absence of detectable aqueous PFOA attenuation at 10 mg/L. Although some microbial consortia can transform or partially defluorinate PFOA, this capacity is typically restricted to narrow physicochemical windows and concentrations [87,92,93]. The abundances of Pseudohongiella, Flavobacterium, and Parvibaculum declined in the salt-marsh-derived consortium under the tested PFOA treatments. Conversely, Pseudomonas persisted in both source-derived consortia despite frequently occurring below the neutral-model prediction. This persistence is consistent with the metabolic versatility of this genus and its documented role in xenobiotic catabolism [94,95,96,97]. The selective enrichment of Sericytochromatia in the freshwater-derived consortium at 10 mg/L PFOA is of particular ecological interest. As a non-photosynthetic sister lineage of cyanobacteria, Sericytochromatia carries genomic signatures of oxidative stress tolerance that may, speculatively, also confer tolerance to PFOA-induced membrane and redox stress [98]. Taken together, these taxonomic shifts indicate source-dependent responses to PFOA in the two enriched consortia. The potential sensitivity of nitrogen-fixing genera such as Bradyrhizobium under PFAS stress also deserves attention. Because nitrogen cycling activity was not measured, the present study cannot determine whether these taxonomic responses affected biological nitrogen input or primary productivity [99,100,101]. Legionella and Pseudomonas are known to thrive in biofilms and can enhance the thickness and rigidity of the biofilm matrix, and PFOA has been shown to stimulate biofilm density and extracellular polysaccharide production that creates a protective physical defense mechanism [102,103].

At the predicted functional level, differences in the representation of housekeeping enzymes and xenobiotic transformation and stress response pathways were consistent with functions commonly associated with microbial stress responses [104,105,106]. The two source-derived consortia nevertheless showed contrasting, seed-dependent predicted functional profiles. The salt-marsh-derived consortium showed predicted enrichment in functions associated with defense, osmoregulation, and extracellular macromolecule processing, including the broad-spectrum proteolytic and hydrolytic enzymes serralysin (EC 3.4.24.40) and creatinase (EC 3.5.3.3) (Figure S6), which are annotated as participating in peptide and guanidino compound utilization [107,108,109]. In contrast, the freshwater-derived consortium showed predicted enrichment in pathways associated with glutathione metabolism and dioxygenase activity, as well as DNA repair pathways. This pattern may reflect greater potential for oxidative stress and xenobiotic response functions [110,111]. The higher predicted representation of taurine/hypotaurine metabolism in the salt-marsh-derived consortium, and its persistence under PFOA exposure, is consistent with a potential role for osmolyte-associated functions under saline conditions. The surfactant properties of PFOA and its reported effects on membrane permeability provide a possible biological context for this predicted pattern [112]. In particular, hypotaurine acts as an effective scavenger of hydroxyl radicals, neutralizing oxidative damage before it can disable ribosomal function or fragment genomic DNA [113]. Together, these predicted signatures are consistent with greater representation of functions associated with membrane maintenance, ion regulation, and antioxidant defense in the salt-marsh-derived community. These predicted functions describe differences between the two enriched consortia and require direct functional measurements for validation. By contrast, the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium showed higher predicted representation of functions associated with cellular repair and xenobiotic oxidation, including glutathione metabolism, dioxygenase activity (e.g., phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase, EC 1.14.12.7), and DNA repair pathways such as non-homologous end joining (ko03450). Glutathione is the central low-molecular-weight antioxidant in many bacteria and defends against the reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under PFOA exposure [114]. The higher predicted representation of glutathione metabolism in the freshwater-derived consortium indicates greater inferred potential for glutathione-associated antioxidant functions. In parallel, PFOA-induced oxidative stress and membrane damage have been reported to elevate rates of horizontal gene transfer in adjacent biofilm communities, with possible implications for the spread of resistance traits [84]. The higher predicted representation of oxidative enzymes may reflect broader xenobiotic response potential, even though the C–F backbone of PFOA itself remains recalcitrant to enzymatic attack. Because Tax4Fun2 infers functional potential from 16S rRNA gene profiles, these results are not measurements of pathway expression or biochemical activity. Confirming that these predicted functions reflect active physiological responses would require direct measurements of ROS and glutathione/GSSG ratios, together with metabolomic, transcriptomic, or proteomic analyses. When these ecological patterns are integrated, in the salt-marsh-derived consortium, PFOA may act as a deterministic filter that inhibits sensitive marine-associated taxa, leaving a smaller community characterized by predicted osmolyte management and extracellular proteolysis functions. By contrast, in the freshwater-derived consortium, PFOA may act as a competitive-release disturbance that relieves dominance and is associated with greater predicted representation of functions related to redox buffering, xenobiotic transformation, and DNA repair. The same chemical exposure was therefore associated with different taxonomic, assembly, and predicted functional patterns in the two source-derived consortia.

The community assembly analyses identified different assembly patterns in the two laboratory-enriched consortia under PFOA exposure. Although incubation time drove both systems toward predominantly stochastic assembly by Day 75, the early stages were marked by strong deterministic filtering, and the PFOA treatments showed the strongest signature in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. Heterogeneous selection dominated the response of the salt-marsh-derived consortium, a pattern consistent with high-stress environments in which environmental filters such as salinity and nutrient limitation strongly dictate community membership [115,116]. Deterministic, niche-based selection acts when environmental conditions filter taxa according to their functional traits [117]. In the salt-marsh-derived consortium, PFOA imposed a stronger deterministic signature than in the freshwater-derived consortium, particularly at 1 mg/L, where heterogeneous selection accounted for approximately two-thirds of the assembly process. This pattern indicates stronger filtering in the salt-marsh-derived community under the tested culture conditions, with only a subset of pre-adapted genotypes occupying the resulting niche. Salinity may have contributed to this pattern, but its effect cannot be separated from microbiome source or other differences between the culture conditions. PFOA thus may operate as an additional selective layer on an already-selective abiotic background, intensifying the role of deterministic processes observed in the βNTI analysis. These results therefore support the view that predicting a community’s response to a contaminant requires explicit knowledge of its baseline assembly regime. The present results suggest that responses to the same PFOA exposure may differ between source-derived consortia under their respective culture conditions [118]. A similar shift from stochastic toward deterministic assembly with increasing contaminant load has also been reported in polluted freshwater systems [119]. Importantly, when PFOA-exposed samples were pooled across both enriched consortia, the neutral community model fit collapsed (Figure 5C; R2 < 0), indicating that PFOA-driven selection can override neutral dispersal at the system level. The collapse is a regime shift effect consistent with the dose-amplified deterministic signature observed in the salt-marsh-derived consortium βNTI (Figure 4A), and with the further increase of drift in the freshwater-derived consortium at 10 mg/L. At the lower 1 mg/L exposure, by contrast, the same chemical perturbation produced clearly seed-dependent effects on assembly. This source-dependent contrast was observed within the tested enrichment system and cannot be used to define field-scale toxicity or remediation criteria. The NCM analysis yielded a higher fitted migration parameter for the freshwater-derived consortium than for the salt-marsh-derived consortium. This difference describes the experimental consortia and should not be interpreted as evidence that the corresponding natural freshwater marsh is more open or better connected. This higher connectivity likely underpins the apparent resilience of the freshwater-marsh-derived consortium, because taxa lost to disturbance can be more readily replaced by stochastic immigration. The negative R2 of the PFOA-pooled NCM fit further indicates that, under PFOA exposure, neutral dispersal alone can no longer explain the occurrence–abundance relationship, consistent with previous observations that environmental stress generally favors pre-tolerant species and reshapes community structure accordingly [120]. In the present case, PFOA acts as a selective agent in addition to the simplified, resource-limited microcosm environment. The magnitude of the deterministic shift associated with PFOA depended on the recipient consortium: the same exposure was associated with a near-neutral perturbation in the freshwater-derived consortium and a stronger selective disturbance in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. The candidate taxa identified in this study are specific to the enriched consortia and require validation in unmanipulated field communities before they can be considered for biomonitoring.

In conclusion, under the tested culture conditions, PFOA produced context-dependent responses in the laboratory-enriched freshwater- and salt-marsh-derived consortia, acting as a near-neutral perturbation in the freshwater-derived consortium and as a strongly selective, niche-based filter in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. Because these consortia were shaped by extraction, defined-media cultivation, and serial transfer, the observed responses should not be extrapolated directly to intact wetland microbial communities under field conditions. The two enriched consortia exhibited contrasting predicted functional profiles, with greater representation of antioxidant defense and DNA repair pathways in the freshwater-derived consortium and of osmolyte management and proteolytic functions in the salt-marsh-derived consortium. These patterns describe contrasting PFOA-associated responses of the two laboratory-enriched, soil-derived microbial consortia under their respective culture conditions and should not be interpreted as differences between intact freshwater marsh and salt marsh microbiomes. In the exploratory alpha diversity analysis, microbial community source and sampling day accounted for most of the observed variation, whereas PFOA concentration showed a nominal overall association only with Shannon diversity. Because interaction terms could not be estimated, the observed source-specific patterns should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence that PFOA produced opposite diversity responses in the two consortia. Whether this pattern extends to other salt-affected systems requires validation using field samples with accompanying physicochemical measurements. Because microbiome source and culture salinity were not separated experimentally, their individual contributions to the observed differences cannot be resolved. Within the experimental system, samples from the two PFOA-exposed consortia deviated from the neutral community model prediction, indicating a stronger contribution of selection relative to neutral dispersal under the tested conditions. This pattern should not be extrapolated to ecosystem-level community assembly. The contrasting responses caution against assuming a single microbial response to PFOA across source-derived enriched consortia, although their relevance to field-scale PFAS risk assessment remains to be established. The source-associated taxa identified here are candidates for future validation and should not yet be considered field biomarkers. Similarly, the possible contribution of biomass- or EPS-mediated biosorption requires direct measurement before it can inform the design of PFAS remediation strategies. These findings provide testable hypotheses for future studies of natural attenuation and wetland-based treatment systems but are insufficient to establish their performance in native wetlands. Future work pairing broader taxonomic characterization and time-resolved metatranscriptomics with quantitative fluorine mass balance across replicated field sites will be needed to determine whether these microcosm patterns occur in unmanipulated sediments and whether the candidate taxa can serve as field biomarkers of PFAS exposure.
